title: Orienta
description:
Orienta — Making EBSD indexing accessible

EBSD pattern analysis for intermetallic phase identification in aluminium alloys

Orienta is a desktop application (Electron + React + FastAPI) that brings the three main families of EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) indexing — Hough/Radon, dictionary, and spherical-harmonic indexing — together in a single graphical interface. It was developed to accelerate the identification of intermetallic phases in aluminium alloys, where closely related candidate phases and complex, large-unit-cell crystal structures make routine indexing difficult, while remaining a general-purpose EBSD tool for any material.

Orienta is built on the kikuchipy / orix / diffsims scientific stack and integrates with EMsoft and EMSphInx as optional external tools (run via WSL), following their published methods. It also adds its own GPU-accelerated forward-simulation and indexing engines. It contains no EMSphInx source code. It does contain tabulated data and two routines ported from EMsoft and from the SHTfile reference implementation (both BSD-3-Clause); these are itemised in the repository’s NOTICE.md, whose licence texts travel with the source.

Indexing
• Hough/Radon indexing via PyEBSDIndex.
• Dictionary indexing on CPU (kikuchipy) and on GPU (a native PyTorch implementation).
• Spherical-harmonic (SHT) indexing, either through the EMSphInx command-line tool or through a native, in-process GPU (PyTorch) reimplementation of the spherical-harmonic indexing method (Lenthe, Singh & De Graef, 2019).
• Automatic pseudo-symmetry resolution for cubic-approximant intermetallics: for phases whose Kikuchi-band geometry is more symmetric than the true crystal (point groups m-3 / 23), the spherical correlation can lock onto a wrong pseudo-symmetric variant. Orienta resolves this with a hybrid approach — it substitutes Hough band-geometry orientations for the affected phase (with a per-pixel fallback where Hough fails) while leaving ordinary phases on the pure spherical result.

Native GPU forward simulation (EMsoft-free)
• A self-contained, hardware-adaptive forward model computes the full EBSD master pattern — Monte-Carlo electron scattering → dynamical master pattern → spherical-harmonic transform — entirely in Python/CUDA, with automatic fallback to CPU. It requires neither EMsoft nor WSL. On the validation cases the GPU master pattern is numerically equivalent to an EMsoft reference (master-pattern NCC ≈ 0.9999); it is not byte-identical and uses a capped electron count by default.

Crystal database and CIF → simulation pipeline
• Convert CIF files to EMsoft .xtal crystal files (pymatgen + spglib), with tabulated Debye–Waller factors (and an editor) and a citation/space-group validity check.
• Generate EBSD master patterns (master.h5) and spherical-harmonic (.sht) files from those .xtal files, using either the native GPU engine or the EMsoft pipeline, into a local crystal database.

EDS integration
• Element maps and a standardless, semi-quantitative Counts → wt% → at% conversion (Cliff–Lorimer with built-in approximate k-factors), intended for rapid chemistry-based phase pre-selection and pixel filtering — not for quantitative microanalysis (publication-quality quantification requires ZAF or standards-based calibration).

Maps, post-processing and visualisation
• Layered phase maps (phase / inverse pole figure / band contrast / confidence index / EDS overlays) with per-layer opacity, blending and composite export.
• MTEX-style post-processing: grain reconstruction, grain-size statistics, KAM/GOS, recrystallisation analysis, texture components with a simplified ODF-based texture index, and multi-sheet Excel export.
• Pole figures, an HDF5 explorer, batch processing of multiple files/phases, and pattern-centre refinement (including a grid-fit per-pixel PC field).
• Lazy loading of multi-gigabyte datasets.

The user interface is available in English, German, Japanese and Chinese.

Data formats: Oxford Instruments H5OINA (primary) and EDAX H5.
Optional acceleration: an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA 12) for the GPU indexing and simulation paths; these fall back to CPU or the external WSL tools when no GPU is present.

License: GPL-3.0-or-later (Orienta derives from GPL-licensed kikuchipy code).

How to cite

If you publish results obtained with Orienta, please cite this archive (see the citation box / DOI above) together with the upstream tools whose methods you used. Orienta is built on a large body of open-source EBSD work:

Core library (Orienta is built on it and inherits its GPL-3.0 license)
• kikuchipy — Ånes, H. W., Crout, P., Lervik, L. A., Natlandsmyr, O., Bergh, T., Hjelen, J., van Helvoort, A. T. J., & Marthinsen, K. (2026). kikuchipy: an open-source toolbox for analysis of EBSD patterns. arXiv:2605.25722 (preprint). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25722 — Software: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3597646

Orientation/symmetry and diffraction utilities
• orix — Johnstone, D. N., Martineau, B. H., Crout, P., Midgley, P. A., & Eggeman, A. S. (2020). Density-based clustering of crystal (mis)orientations and the orix Python library. Journal of Applied Crystallography, 53(5), 1293–1298. https://doi.org/10.1107/S1600576720011103 — Software: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3459662
• diffsims — Software: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3337900

Hough/Radon indexing
• PyEBSDIndex — Rowenhorst, D. J., Callahan, P. G., & Ånes, H. W. (2024). Fast Radon transforms for high-precision EBSD orientation determination using PyEBSDIndex. Journal of Applied Crystallography, 57(1), 3–19. https://doi.org/10.1107/S1600576723010221

Spherical-harmonic indexing and pseudo-symmetry handling (the EMSphInx method, independently reimplemented in Orienta)
• Lenthe, W. C., Singh, S., & De Graef, M. (2019). A spherical harmonic transform approach to the indexing of electron back-scattered diffraction patterns. Ultramicroscopy, 207, 112841. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultramic.2019.112841
• Lenthe, W. C., Singh, S., & De Graef, M. (2019). Prediction of potential pseudo-symmetry issues in the indexing of electron backscatter diffraction patterns. Journal of Applied Crystallography, 52(5), 1157–1168. https://doi.org/10.1107/S1600576719011233

Dynamical pattern simulation (the EMsoft method, used by the optional EMsoft engine)
• Callahan, P. G., & De Graef, M. (2013). Dynamical Electron Backscatter Diffraction Patterns. Part I: Pattern Simulations. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 19(5), 1255–1265. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1431927613001840
• EMsoft — Singh, S., Ram, F., & De Graef, M. (2017). EMsoft: open source software for electron diffraction/image simulations. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 23(S1), 212–213. https://doi.org/10.1017/S143192761700174X — Software: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2581284
